items.title: Brazil's Black Monday: EWZ -25% intraday, -18% close on Lula's win
items.idea: MSCI Brazil ETF fell almost 25% intraday and closed -18% - a 1987-scale crash (S&P -20.5%). The real had its worst day since the 1999 float, bigger than the day the peg broke. Prediction markets still gave Lula ~20%, yet stock and bond investors priced ~100% Bolsonaro.
items.angle: Look at who was wrong: not the polls (too close to call) but positioning. When a 20% event moves an ETF 18%, the market was holding a one-sided book, and that is a tradable signal for every other contested election.
items.tweetA: Prediction markets had Lula at 20%. EWZ closed -18%. Somebody was pricing 100% on a 1-in-5 event, and it wasn't the polls. The real got a bigger shock than the day Brazil abandoned its peg.
items.tweetB: Black Monday 1987 took 20.5% off the S&P. Brazil's ETF lost 25% intraday on an election the polls called a coin flip. The lesson isn't Lula, it's what foreign passive money holds into binary events. $EWZ

charts.desc: Authers has 4+ charts: ETF vs Black Monday, BRL vs 1999 peg break, cross-asset reversal, Variant Perception contentious-election returns. The BRL chart is the one.

items.title: Foreign investors hold only ~10% of Brazilian real debt - this isn't 1999
items.idea: SocGen: foreigners own about 10% of BRL-denominated debt after two decades of building domestic capital pools. Variant Perception's chart shows large equity returns in the year after contentious elections. Marc Chandler would buy local bonds yielding ~12.8%; SocGen prefers the currency since a hawkish central bank supports the real.
items.angle: Fade-the-flow framework: Latin American equity is driven by foreign passive flows that sell left-wing wins, while the domestic bid has grown. Watch whether BCB goes hawkish.
items.tweetA: Everyone is comparing Brazil to 1999. In 1999 foreigners held the debt. Today it's ~10%. The currency can crash; the funding model can't, because the holders are Brazilians in reais. 12.8% carry is the question.
items.tweetB: Variant's chart: contentious-election selloffs in LatAm get bought within the year. The setup is always the same: passive foreign flows panic, domestic capital shrugs. Lula isn't the trade, the flow reversal is. $EWZ $BRL

charts.desc: Variant Perception returns-after-contentious-elections chart; SocGen foreign share of BRL debt chart.

items.title: Trump says Brazil result 'looks rigged'; Bolsonaro demands annulment
items.idea: Authers cites Bolsonaro seeking to annul the result and Trump saying it 'looks rigged' as the reasons beyond fiscal fears. The margin is 3.6 points and Signum's Rafael Ch expects courts to avoid annulment, with targeted supplementary voting more likely. Lula promised a 15% rise in welfare payments; Bolsonaro's Liberals hold more than a third of the Senate.
items.angle: Political tail risk is the part not in the price. If courts decline annulment, the unrest premium unwinds; a US president contesting a foreign election is a new variable for US-LatAm relations.
items.tweetA: The US president is now publicly contesting another country's election result. A 3.6-point margin, a judiciary that won't annul, and a currency that already priced the worst. Which of those is the asymmetric part?
items.tweetB: One-third of the Senate for Bolsonaro's party means Lula can't spend freely. The market priced the 15% welfare increase as if it were law. It isn't. Constraints matter more than promises.

items.title: Anthropic S-1: $16.3B H1 revenue vs $1.2B a year ago, 19% operating margin
items.idea: Per the filing as cited by Bloomberg: H1 2026 revenue $16.3B vs $1.2B in H1 2025 (13.6x), Q2 adjusted operating margin 19%, $3.9B operating cash flow in H1. IPO could top SpaceX's $75B June raise. Debut is the test of investors' willingness to keep funding the AI boom.
items.angle: Fundamentals outrun the sector: a profitable AI lab IPOs into a selloff driven by depleting FCF and debt-investor demands. A strong print could mask weakness elsewhere.
items.tweetA: $1.2B to $16.3B in six months of comparison. 19% operating margin. This isn't a cash-burning story, which is exactly why it's a dangerous comp for everyone else about to raise: Anthropic's numbers won't transfer to them.
items.tweetB: The SpaceX raise was $75B in June. Anthropic wants more, into a market where momentum has just had its worst weeks in decades. If it prices well, the read is 'Anthropic is special', not 'AI is fine'. Trade the dispersion.

items.title: OpenAI cut ~$150B from its valuation, now $1.25T, as investors pushed back
items.idea: Bloomberg link in Authers: OpenAI shaved about $150B off its valuation in a funding round after investor pushback, landing at $1.25T. It can ill afford a weak Anthropic debut and it's unclear how long it can stay private given capital needs. Bloomberg Economics: when capex exceeds operating cash flow, firms without reserves must raise externally.
items.angle: Private-market ceiling is visible: the lab with the largest compute obligations just took a haircut, while the profitable one goes public.
items.tweetA: OpenAI took a $150B haircut in a private round. Anthropic is going public with positive operating cash flow. The market is telling you which AI business model it will finance and which it will merely tolerate.
items.tweetB: When capex exceeds operating cash flow, you live at the mercy of funding conditions. Hyperscalers have reserves. Labs don't. Every basis point on the credit spread is now an AI variable.

items.title: Anthropic S&M spend: $239M to $3,808M in one year
items.idea: BowTiedBull flags sales and marketing growing from $239M to $3.8B (~16x), calling it an unprecedented step function for a tech company. He speculates it's user acquisition ahead of the IPO. Net revenue retention is described as 'insanely good'.
items.angle: S&M at 3.8B vs H1 revenue of 16.3B is ~23% of revenue, a distribution buildout, not just API economics. Check whether this includes channel/cloud partner fees.
items.tweetA: Anthropic S&M: $239M to $3.8B. That's a 16x. Product-led growth companies don't do that; this looks like an enterprise go-to-market being bought at speed. Retention will show whether it was worth it.
items.tweetB: Watch the S&M line, not the revenue line. A company growing 13x with a 16x S&M increase has a CAC story the S-1 hasn't told yet.

charts.desc: Source tables from the S-1 (S&M, retention, customer concentration) - worth opening.

items.title: $6.6M revenue/employee, ~11,900 customers paying $100K+, $321.4B in commitments
items.idea: Revenue per employee is roughly $6.6M; about 11,900 customers pay $100K+ and BowTiedBull sees room for 5-20x. Lease/compute commitments total $321.4B against a planned $100B raise. Caveat: convertible debt and the Broadcom agreement let it defer cash outlay, distorting margins.
items.angle: The $321.4B vs $100B gap is the whole thesis: revenue has to outgrow commitments by a lot. Convertibles may sit in compute cost, making true gross margin unknowable.
items.tweetA: $321B of commitments against a $100B raise. Customer count at $100K+ is 11,900. For the math to work, that cohort has to be 10x bigger in three years. Possible, but that's the bet being sold.
items.tweetB: $6.6M of revenue per employee. Microsoft is at roughly $1.2M and is offering buyouts to a quarter of its staff. One of those curves is the future of corporate headcount.

items.title: Microsoft offers buyouts to >25% of employees; 60,000 heads implies $855K savings each to cover AI capex
items.idea: MSFT has ~223K employees (34.5% R&D, 39.9% operations, 19.3% S&M). BowTiedBull does the math: capex rose $51.3B; if 60,000 heads leave, you need $855K saved per employee in one year, ~$285K over three. At about a year of pay per severance package, payback is 3-4 years.
items.angle: AI capex is being justified by headcount cuts because cost savings are measurable while AI revenue isn't. Every other mega-cap now has cover to cut and blame AI.
items.tweetA: $51.3B of extra capex divided by 60,000 buyouts is $855K per head. That is the number Microsoft's CFO is staring at. AI doesn't have to make money, it has to replace salaries. See who is next.
items.tweetB: Microsoft gave the template: buy out a quarter of staff, call it AI efficiency, and let the capex ledger read as a cost play. Every other CFO under capex pressure just got permission. $MSFT

items.title: Take the first severance wave: 2001 and 2008 pattern
items.idea: Rule of thumb: first-round packages are the richest, laid-off pools are smaller, and smaller firms hire from them to wait out the storm. In 2008 the second Q1-after cuts hit people who then struggled to find roles as hiring dried up.
items.angle: If the AI layoff cycle resembles 2001/2008, we're at the start. A cultural shift: the optimal career move becomes volunteering to be cut first.
items.tweetA: Second-round layoff victims in 2008 couldn't get hired because nobody was. First-round victims got severance and a market. If MSFT is round one of AI cuts, the incentive is to leave early. That's a labor-market signal.
items.tweetB: Notice the behavioural shift: employees now rationally want to be in the first wave. Buyout take-up rates at Microsoft will tell you how people read the next 12 months.

items.title: AI is loved abroad, doubted at home: Nigeria and Vietnam ~9 in 10 positive, US/Canada/France net negative
items.idea: Economist/GlobeScan 34-country poll: nearly nine in ten in Nigeria and Vietnam say AI will improve their lives, China mid-80s, Indonesia/Kenya/India in the 70s, Brazil/Mexico high 60s, UK barely net positive, US/Canada/France net negative. Gallup/Microsoft: positive beat negative in 34 of 37 countries; the US was the most concerned, with only 36% seeing AI as mostly helpful.
items.angle: The consumer AI race will be won with users who are more enthusiastic and poorer than Americans. That favours free, good-enough models, including Chinese open ones.
items.tweetA: The AI backlash is a Western phenomenon. 90% positive in Vietnam and Nigeria, net negative in the US and France. If your model for AI demand is based on American sentiment, you're using the wrong map.
items.tweetB: 'Pessimism is a privilege for those who can afford to despair.' The next billion AI users are in places that can't. They will determine which model wins, and it won't be the one priced at $200/month.

charts.desc: Animated chart of country sentiment spectrum (Vietnam to France) at top of the post - tweet-worthy.

items.title: The usage paradox: rich countries use AI more and like it less
items.idea: Microsoft data: 18.8% of working-age people used gen AI in Q2; Global North 28.8% vs South 16.2%; UAE 73%, Singapore 64%. Kenya: ~9% usage but 85% say AI will help. US: 32% never tried AI vs 57% median across 37 countries, and 68% of daily US users still worry.
items.angle: Familiarity breeds worry in the West, but usage slowly reduces it (68% daily vs 80% infrequent users). It is the 'selling AI on fear' hypothesis.
items.tweetA: Kenya: 9% use AI, 85% expect it to help. US: 68% of daily users are still worried. Usage in rich countries isn't curing fear, it's confirming it. The sales pitch is the problem. 'Use AI or lose your job' is not a product.
items.tweetB: UAE 73%, Singapore 64%, US a third. The countries with state-led AI adoption and no job-loss narrative use it the most. Narrative is a competitive variable.

items.title: Why the West differs: fear is the sales pitch
items.idea: Four drivers per Economist/Parekh: less to lose in informal economies; living memory of fast tech change (payments, smartphones); demographics (East Asia hopes AI/robots replace missing workers); and framing: US leaders warn of extinction and job loss, while Asian leaders talk about what people can do with AI. Mumbai shopkeepers using ChatGPT for ads reported higher sales.
items.angle: Demographics plus favourable sentiment make East Asia the natural Physical AI deployment market. Narrative risk is a business risk for the US IPO class.
items.tweetA: Asian tech bosses rarely discuss AI doom. American ones lead with it. Samsung sells a tool, OpenAI sells an apocalypse. Same models, different brand equity, and the Anthropic/OpenAI IPOs have to sell to the doubters.
items.tweetB: An ageing East Asia wants robots because it lacks workers. America fears robots because it has them. Same technology, opposite demographic sign. Where does Physical AI scale first?

items.title: Data-center backlash: Goldman counts 86 projects cancelled or delayed this year, 76 over local opposition
items.idea: Parekh cites Goldman's tally of 86 US data center projects cancelled or delayed in 2026, 76 due to local opposition. Early signs abroad: hundreds protest an Amazon hyperscale data center in Thane near Mumbai; marchers in the Philippines target 'Pax Silica', the US-led AI/chip supply chain initiative.
items.angle: Permitting and social licence are becoming the binding constraint on AI buildout, and a midterms issue. Power-adjacent names with grandfathered sites gain scarcity value.
items.tweetA: 76 of 86 cancelled or delayed data centers died on local opposition, not chips and not capital. The bottleneck moved from silicon to zoning boards. Who owns already-permitted sites? $VRT $ETN
items.tweetB: Backlash is spreading from US counties to Thane and Manila. Every announced gigawatt assumes a permit nobody has been asked for yet. Capex guidance and local politics are now one model.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / Goldman (Bobby Molavi)
items.title: Goldman: momentum unwind more violent than 2000, 2009 or 2020; market 'unplayable'
items.idea: Goldman's Molavi describes the last 2-3 weeks as unplayable: S&P near records, but factor and momentum sessions have been worse than several notorious crises. Selling has spread across factors, sectors and crowded strategies, with retreat to quality and defensives. Goldman sees signs the worst of the liquidation may be near but that confidence will take longer to return.
items.angle: Index vol hides dispersion: PMs are being killed beneath a calm index. A liquidation end doesn't mean a V-recovery - the reset is in gross exposure.
items.tweetA: S&P near highs. Momentum worse than 2000, 2009 and 2020. Both can be true when the index is carried by a handful of names while everything else gets de-grossed. Calm index, violent book.
items.tweetB: Goldman says liquidation may be ending but confidence takes longer. That's the part to trade: after forced selling stops, the buyers need a reason to return, and there isn't an obvious one until the Anthropic IPO prices.

items.title: 2000 analog: tech-down, staples-up clusters have appeared twice in 2026
items.idea: In 2000 the Nasdaq-100 peaked March 27, then clusters of days with tech -2.5%+ while staples rose appeared, preceding a 36% drop, a summer bounce, then a deeper decline. TMAD finds two 2026 clusters: June 5-July 2 (XLK -6.66% on June 5, QQQ ~$740 to $705; June 23 XLK -3.36% / XLP +1.65%) and Oct 14-22. Many AI names are already down 50%+ while indices hold near highs.
items.angle: A pattern-recognition frame - count rotation days, check new highs breadth. The author says it doesn't require calling a crash, since dead-cat bounces are common.
items.tweetA: XLK -6.66% in one day in June. Tech down, staples up, repeated twice this year. In 2000 that pattern showed up right after the Nasdaq peak. Not saying it's 2000, saying the index is the last place to see it.
items.tweetB: AI names down 50%+ from peak, the index at highs. In 2000 the same divergence lasted months before the index caught down. Count the rotation days, not the headlines. $XLK $XLP

charts.desc: Cluster charts comparing 2000 and 2026 rotation days; charts inside - worth opening.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / UBS (Jason Perl)
items.title: Gold's $4,082.80 question: speculators exhausted, China still buying kilobars early
items.idea: UBS: gold is caught between exhausted speculative positioning and persistent physical demand. The heaviest selling was one session; China's kilobar demand is arriving earlier than usual and refinery capacity is hard to secure. Technical strategist Perl turned bullish after completing his minimum correction target; $4,082.80 must clear to confirm recovery. Silver stays neutral.
items.angle: Physical vs paper divergence: Chinese buyers are indifferent to leverage unwinds. Refinery capacity as a hidden bottleneck.
items.tweetA: Last week's gold liquidation was one session. Chinese kilobar demand is arriving early and refiners are booked out. Paper gold is shaking out leverage while physical buyers are locking in supply. Watch $4,082.
items.tweetB: Silver stays neutral at UBS and is 'unusually sensitive to headlines'. Gold has a physical floor; silver has a speculative one. When both are shaken, only one has someone buying the dip with cash.
